title: Pre-work surface assessment and test patches
audience: Stone and terrazzo restoration technicians and leading hands who assess a surface and decide the method before any abrasive, chemical or sealing step
learningOutcomes: Record the material, finish, condition and location of a stone or terrazzo surface before work
Identify cracks, loose edges, joints and previous treatments that change the method
Run a test patch that uses the same dust and water controls as the full job
Decide to proceed, change the method or stop, based on the recorded test result
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: Safe Work Australia, Working with silica and silica containing products (national guidance) (February 2022).

instruction.heading: Assess before you abrade
instruction.body: Once the material is confirmed as natural stone or terrazzo, record what the surface is like before any tool touches it. Write down the material, the finish (polished, honed, flamed, tumbled or textured), the condition (etching, staining, scratches, chips, cracks, sealer residue, previous repairs, lifting or loose areas), the location, the traffic and the moisture. Note any fixtures, joints, penetrations and edges. Cracks and loose edges matter because a grinder or a pad can break them, and the break makes dust and a hazard. Use good light and a torch from a low angle to see the surface, and take photographs. These checks are visual and do not damage the surface. Do not use a scratch or cut to find out more about the surface, because that creates dust and changes what you are trying to assess.

instruction.heading: Test patches that show the real response
instruction.body: A test patch is a small area, usually in a concealed place such as under a fixture or inside a cupboard, that is treated with the proposed method before the whole job is started. The patch shows how the stone responds to the abrasive, the water, the chemical and the contact time. Record the abrasive grit or pad, the machine speed as set by the manufacturer, the water use, any chemical and its contact time, and the result. Look for colour change, scratch pattern, etching, staining, edge rounding and any change in sheen. The test patch must use the same dust controls as the full job, including the wet method and extraction set out in “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”. A test is never a reason to start dry work. If the patch dusts, stop, add the control, and then repeat the test.

instruction.heading: Deciding the method from the result
instruction.body: After the test, decide one of three things. Proceed when the patch gives the expected result and the controls are in place. Change the method when the patch shows a risk, for example a sequence with a finer grit, a different pad, a different product or a shorter contact time. Stop when the patch shows damage that cannot be managed, when the material is not identified (see “Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone”), when a crack or loose edge would be affected, or when a control cannot be set up. Write the chosen method, the grit or product sequence and the controls on the job record. If the result is uncertain, tell the client in writing what is known and what is not, before the work starts. A passing test does not identify the material, and it does not replace the identification record.

procedure: Photograph the whole surface, the edges, the joints and any existing damage before work.
Record the material, finish, condition, location, traffic and moisture on the assessment sheet.
Confirm the identification basis from “Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone” and do not proceed if it is not identified.
Check for cracks, loose tiles or chips, grout failure, and edges that could break under the tool.
Select a concealed test location and record its position.
Set up the controls from “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping” and run the test patch with the same method as the full job.
Record the test result, decide to proceed, change or stop, and write the decision on the job record.
If the result is uncertain, give the client written notes before work starts.

workedExamples.situation: A polished terrazzo floor in a school hall has a pale ring around a chair leg. The technician tests a concealed patch with a fine diamond pad and water. The ring fades, but the area around the patch looks duller than before.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the technician proceed to the full floor with the same method, and what should be recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: The test shows that the method removes the ring but also dulls the finish. Proceeding unchanged would spread the dulling across the floor. The technician records the test result, changes the sequence to a finer step for the final pass, and re-tests before the full area. The client receives a written note that the ring may fade but the finish will need restoration after the final pass. The school's requirements for access and noise are checked through the site induction and the client.

equipmentAndPpe: Torch or daylight lamp for a low-angle view
Camera or phone with date stamp
Test patch materials as set by the method in “Honing and polishing sequence for natural stone and terrazzo”
Dust controls from “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping” for the test as well as the full job
Respiratory protection planned per “Respirators, fit testing and health monitoring” for any residual risk

commonErrors.error: Skipping the test patch because the job looks familiar.
commonErrors.prevention: Each stone and finish responds differently. Test each job, even when the material is the same as the last job.

commonErrors.error: Recording the surface as 'marble' or 'granite' only.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the finish, condition and location, as well as the material and the basis of identification.

commonErrors.error: Running the test patch dry because it is small.
commonErrors.prevention: The test uses the same controls as the full job. A small dry test still creates silica dust.

commonErrors.error: Treating a passing test as proof of the material.
commonErrors.prevention: A test shows the response of the surface to a method. Identification is recorded separately under “Confirm the surface before work: natural stone, terrazzo or engineered stone”.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Test patches use the same dust and water controls as the full job. A test is not a reason to start any dry, dust-generating work, and this lesson does not change the silica duties in “Respirable crystalline silica: where it comes from and why it matters” and “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”.

Stop-work rule: stop if the surface is not identified as natural stone or terrazzo, if a crack or loose edge would be affected by the method, or if a test patch shows damage that the method cannot manage.
This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate or authority to carry out stone restoration.

qualityStandard: An assessment record with photographs is completed before the first abrasive, chemical or sealing step.
The test patch is recorded with the method, the result and its location.
The decision to proceed, change or stop is written on the job record.
Uncertain results are explained to the client in writing before work starts.
documentationEvidence: Assessment sheet with material, finish, condition, location and moisture
Dated photographs of the surface, edges and existing damage
Test patch log with method, grit or product, water use, contact time and result
Decision record and client note where the result is uncertain
summary: Assess the surface and record its finish, condition, location and moisture before work.
Check cracks and loose edges, because the tool can break them and create dust.
Run a test patch with the same controls as the full job.
Decide to proceed, change the method or stop, and record the decision.
A passing test does not identify the material.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: Safe Work Australia, Working with silica and silica containing products (national guidance) (February 2022).

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the purpose of a test patch?
options: To measure the silica level in the air around the work area and the whole site today
To prove that a licence is held by the business and the crew on the job site today
To check how the surface responds to the proposed method before the full area is treated
To speed up the dust removal on the whole job site, the roof, the yard and the path

knowledgeChecks.question: Which record is required for each test patch?
options: Only the client's name, the address, the phone, the email, the date and the time
The price only, as quoted to the client for the whole job and the stone type
A worker's photograph only, taken on the phone at the site on the day of the test
The method, grit or product, water use, contact time, result and location

knowledgeChecks.question: A test patch creates a dry dust cloud. What should happen?
options: Stop, add the wet method or extraction, and repeat the test
Continue, because the patch is small and does not matter
Use compressed air to clear the dust from the patch
Ignore the cloud and record nothing about it today at all

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a cracked or loose edge matter at assessment?
options: It is only decorative and does not affect the work at all
It can break under a grinder or pad, creating dust and a hazard
It increases the price of the job for the client and the whole crew
It has no safety meaning for the job or the crew at all

knowledgeChecks.question: A surface is unlabelled, its identification is uncertain, and the test patch looks fine. What is the correct decision?
options: Proceed because the test was fine on the surface today
Proceed with a stronger acid to lift the marks off the stone
Stop, because a passing test does not identify the material
Proceed and record that the test was good for now at the site
